prompt.context: Our client is an electronics warehouse selling all kinds of electronics and home appliances. It was founded in 1990 and currently owns 375 stores located in all major cities across the US. They have a healthy profit margin and represent a major player in the electronics retail market, but the CEO hired us to help them grow even quicker. Recently they opened a number of smaller conceptual stores and these stores are less profitable than the regular ones. We have the task to help them grow aggressively while maintaining the profitability.
prompt.question: What are the key areas to investigate in order to determine why the new stores are not profitable? Additionally, how many stores do they need to open in order to secure a 20% market share in 5 years?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current size of the electronics retail market?
What is the client's current market share?
What will the electronics retail market size be in 5 years?
What does aggressive growth mean in terms of market share?
clarifying_info.a: Achieving 20% market share in the next 5 years

clarifying_info.q: Should I assume all current stores have the same revenue and future stores will have the same average revenue?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, for simplicity assume current stores are all the same revenue size and future ones will have the same average revenues

framework: Revenues: type of products sold, assortment, number of customers, customer profile (income, family status) and whether assortment meets their needs
Costs: fixed costs relative to volume sold, labor costs (potentially higher-trained personnel), distribution costs from suppliers to store
Competition: presence of competitors in the area, type of competitor stores in the area
Other: number of hours open, type of stores, location of stores, customer needs and how well the client meets them

questions.prompt: What are the key areas to investigate to determine why the new (smaller conceptual) stores are not profitable?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies revenue drivers (product mix, assortment, customer traffic, customer profile), cost drivers (fixed cost burden relative to smaller volume, labor, distribution), competitive dynamics in the local area, and operational factors (store hours, location, format fit to customer needs).

questions.prompt: How many stores does the client need to open to secure a 20% market share in 5 years?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate current revenue, target revenue, revenue gap, and divide by revenue per store. Candidate should also note that the result (625 additional stores) is not feasible given the company took ~18 years to open 375 stores.

math.setup: Current revenue = current market share × current market size. Revenue per store = current revenue ÷ number of stores. Target revenue = target market share × future market size. Additional revenue needed = target revenue − current revenue. Number of new stores needed = additional revenue needed ÷ revenue per store.
math.answer: 625 new stores needed; however note new stores are smaller/specialized with lower revenue, so actual number would be higher. This is likely not feasible — the client took ~18 years to open 375 stores.

questions.prompt: Is the current strategy (opening smaller conceptual stores) a successful one?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that 625 new stores in 5 years is not feasible given historical pace (~18 years for 375 stores), and that smaller/specialized stores with lower revenues make the target even harder to hit. The current strategy needs to be reconsidered.

brainstorming.prompt: How can the client achieve its aggressive growth objectives if opening new stores alone is not feasible?

categories.name: Store format / expansion
ideas: Open only the old (larger) type of stores which have higher revenues
Choose locations with specific customer profiles (income, family status, hobbies) to maximize revenue per store

categories.name: Product and assortment
ideas: Use the existing customer database to cross-sell and upsell

categories.name: B2B / institutional
ideas: Make contracts with schools, institutions, hotels, and other organizations
Become a distributor for small electronics stores

categories.name: Services
ideas: Start selling services such as repairs and installations

categories.name: Inorganic growth
ideas: Acquire or merge with a competitor

recommendation: The current strategy of opening smaller conceptual stores is insufficient and likely not feasible to reach 20% market share in 5 years — the math requires 625 new stores which exceeds historical build rate
The client should pursue a combination of fewer but larger-format stores, channel diversification (online), B2B contracts, and services to close the revenue gap without relying solely on store count
risks: Larger stores require more capital and longer lead times
Online channel requires significant investment and faces intense competition
B2B contracts may have thin margins
next_steps: Model the revenue contribution of each growth lever to build a realistic 5-year plan
Diagnose root causes of smaller store underperformance before deciding whether to continue or exit that format
Assess acquisition targets to accelerate market share gain inorganically
